claims.text: Moderate or slow heating and cooling rates can produce stable single-phase solid-solution noble-metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements.
Prolonged thermal transients provide sufficient time for multi-element interdiffusion within nanoparticle cores.
Greater interdiffusion during prolonged thermal transients produces a more uniform elemental distribution.
Uniform elemental mixing stabilizes a single-phase solid solution.
Rapid heating and cooling ramps limit atomic diffusion and cause incomplete mixing.
Rapid thermal ramps favor elemental segregation or phase separation.
Rapid thermal ramps produce nanoparticle morphology instabilities.
Heating and cooling ramp rates will be varied from approximately 1 °C/min to 20 °C/min while composition, environment, and precursor processing remain constant.
The final temperature and dwell time will be identical across ramp-rate conditions.
Slower ramps will yield predominantly single-phase nanoparticles with minimal elemental segregation.
Faster ramps will increase the likelihood of multiple phases or compositional inhomogeneity.
Prior reports establish a single-phase high-entropy-alloy nanoparticle baseline.
The prior single-phase baseline was synthesized at moderate ramp rates.
The proposed ramp-rate mechanism applies broadly to inert-atmosphere noble-metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements.
Particle sizes at the extremes or drastically altered compositions may respond differently to ramp-rate changes.
Formation of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles can depend on cooling-rate control.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and boundary specify more than five elements, whereas the initial-state field uses ≥5 elements, which also includes exactly five-element alloys.
